lesson.intro: Every \emph{equivalent expressions} question asks the same thing in different clothing: rewrite an expression in a new form without changing its value for any allowed input. The Digital SAT tests this constantly --- expanding and multiplying polynomials, factoring, simplifying and combining rational expressions, and rewriting powers and radicals. Nothing here requires clever tricks; it requires knowing which moves are legal and applying them in a sensible order.

blocks.title: What equivalent means
blocks.body: Two expressions are equivalent when they produce the same value for every value of the variable for which both are defined. That definition gives you a free checking tool: substitute a convenient number such as $x=2$ into the original expression and into each answer choice, and the choices that disagree are gone. It also explains the phrase ``for $x\neq 3$'' that so often appears in the stem --- the two forms agree everywhere except where the original was undefined.

blocks.title: Multiplying polynomials
blocks.body: Multiplication distributes over addition, so every term of the first factor must multiply every term of the second. For two binomials that means four products; for a binomial times a trinomial it means six. After multiplying, collect like terms --- terms with the identical power of the variable. $x^2$ and $x$ are never like terms, and neither are $x$ and a constant.

blocks.title: The three products worth memorising
blocks.body: \begin{align*} (a+b)^2 &= a^2+2ab+b^2\\ (a-b)^2 &= a^2-2ab+b^2\\ (a+b)(a-b) &= a^2-b^2 \end{align*} Read them left to right to expand and right to left to factor. The middle term $2ab$ in the first two is the one students lose; the missing middle term in the third is the reason a difference of squares factors so cleanly.

blocks.title: $(a+b)^2$ is not $a^2+b^2$
blocks.body: Squaring a sum is not squaring each piece. $(2x-5)^2=4x^2-20x+25$, not $4x^2+25$. The same warning covers radicals and reciprocals: $\sqrt{a+b}\neq\sqrt a+\sqrt b$ and $\dfrac{1}{a+b}\neq\dfrac1a+\dfrac1b$. Every one of these test writers' favourite distractors comes from applying an operation term by term when the operation does not distribute.

blocks.title: Factoring, in the order you should try it
blocks.body: First pull out the greatest common factor: $3x^2-12=3\left(x^2-4\right)$. Then look at what is left. If it is a difference of squares, split it: $x^2-4=(x+2)(x-2)$. If it is a trinomial $x^2+bx+c$, find two numbers with product $c$ and sum $b$. If the leading coefficient is not $1$, as in $6x^2-x-15$, find two numbers with product $ac=-90$ and sum $b=-1$ --- here $9$ and $-10$ --- split the middle term and group. Factoring is finished only when no factor can be factored further.

blocks.title: Cancelling is dividing by a common factor
blocks.body: In a fraction you may cancel only a factor that multiplies the \emph{entire} numerator and the \emph{entire} denominator. So $\dfrac{(x+2)(x-3)}{(x+2)}=x-3$ is legal, but $\dfrac{x+2}{x+4}$ cannot become $\dfrac{2}{4}$ --- those are terms of a sum. This is why the first move on any rational expression is to factor top and bottom completely; until you have factored, you have nothing to cancel.

blocks.title: Adding and subtracting rational expressions
blocks.body: Rewrite each fraction over a common denominator, then combine numerators only. For $\dfrac{2}{x+1}+\dfrac{3}{x}$ the common denominator is $x(x+1)$, so the fractions become $\dfrac{2x}{x(x+1)}$ and $\dfrac{3(x+1)}{x(x+1)}$ and the sum is $\dfrac{5x+3}{x^2+x}$. When subtracting, put the second numerator in parentheses first: the minus sign applies to all of it.

blocks.title: Exponent and radical rules
blocks.body: \begin{align*} x^a\cdot x^b &= x^{a+b} & \frac{x^a}{x^b} &= x^{a-b} & \left(x^a\right)^b &= x^{ab}\\ (xy)^a &= x^ay^a & x^{-a} &= \frac{1}{x^a} & x^{m/n} &= \sqrt[n]{x^m}=\left(\sqrt[n]{x}\right)^m \end{align*} For radicals, factor out the largest perfect square: $\sqrt{72x^2}=\sqrt{36x^2}\cdot\sqrt2=6x\sqrt2$ for $x>0$. Radical terms add only when the radicands match: $4\sqrt3-2\sqrt3=2\sqrt3$.

blocks.title: Exponents on coefficients and the add/multiply mix-up
blocks.body: An outside exponent lands on the coefficient too: $\left(2x^3\right)^3=8x^9$, not $6x^9$, and $\left(8x^6\right)^{2/3}=4x^4$, not $\frac{16}{3}x^4$. And keep the two rules apart --- multiplying powers \emph{adds} exponents while a power of a power \emph{multiplies} them. $x^5\cdot x^3=x^8$, but $\left(x^5\right)^3=x^{15}$.

blocks.title: Plug in a number when the algebra gets long
blocks.body: If the choices are all expressions in $x$, pick a small number that is legal in every expression (avoid $0$, $1$ and anything that makes a denominator zero --- $x=2$ or $x=3$ usually works), evaluate the original, then evaluate the choices. Only the equivalent one matches. This costs about thirty seconds and never requires you to factor anything; it is the fastest route through a hard rational-expression item, and it is a perfect check when you have done the algebra and are not sure.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: a rational expression
blocks.body: \textbf{For $x\neq 2$ and $x\neq -2$, which expression is equivalent to $\dfrac{x^2-x-6}{x^2-4}$?}\\[2pt] \textbf{Step 1 --- factor the numerator.} Two numbers with product $-6$ and sum $-1$ are $-3$ and $2$, so $x^2-x-6=(x-3)(x+2)$.\\ \textbf{Step 2 --- factor the denominator.} It is a difference of squares: $x^2-4=(x+2)(x-2)$.\\ \textbf{Step 3 --- cancel the common factor.} The expression is $\dfrac{(x-3)(x+2)}{(x+2)(x-2)}$, and $x+2$ is a factor of both, so it cancels: $\dfrac{x-3}{x-2}$.\\ \textbf{Step 4 --- check.} Put $x=3$ into the original: $\dfrac{9-3-6}{9-4}=0$. Put $x=3$ into $\dfrac{x-3}{x-2}$: $\dfrac{0}{1}=0$. They agree. Note what was \emph{not} legal: cancelling $x^2$ against $x^2$, since those are terms, not factors.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: matching coefficients
blocks.body: \textbf{The equation $(3x+a)(2x+b)=6x^2+19x+15$ is true for all $x$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers. What is $a+b$?}\\[2pt] \textbf{Step 1 --- expand the left side.} $(3x+a)(2x+b)=6x^2+3bx+2ax+ab=6x^2+(2a+3b)x+ab$.\\ \textbf{Step 2 --- match coefficients.} ``True for all $x$'' means the two sides are the same polynomial, so corresponding coefficients are equal: $2a+3b=19$ and $ab=15$.\\ \textbf{Step 3 --- test the factor pairs of $15$.} The positive pairs are $(1,15)$, $(3,5)$, $(5,3)$, $(15,1)$. Only $a=5$, $b=3$ gives $2(5)+3(3)=19$.\\ \textbf{Step 4 --- answer the question asked.} It asks for $a+b$, not for $a$: the answer is $8$. Notice that getting the constant term right is not enough --- the middle term is what selects the pair.

problems.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $(x+3)(x+5)$?
problems.solution: Each term of the first factor multiplies each term of the second, so there are four products. The two middle products $5x$ and $3x$ are like terms and must be combined; a student who multiplies only the first terms and only the last terms gets $x^2+15$ and loses the entire middle term.

problems.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $3x(2x^2-4x+5)$?
problems.solution: The distributive property sends the factor $3x$ to \emph{every} term inside the parentheses, and the variable multiplies too: $3x\cdot 5=15x$, not $15$. Stopping the distribution early is the mistake behind the other choices.

problems.stem: The expression $(2x+3)(x-1)$ can be written in the form $2x^2+bx-3$, where $b$ is a constant. What is the value of $b$?
problems.solution: Two expressions are equivalent only when every matching coefficient agrees, so $b$ is simply the coefficient of $x$ in the expanded product. Expanding gives $-2x+3x=x$, so $b=1$ --- not $-2$ or $3$ alone.

problems.stem: Which of the following is equivalent to $x^2-9$?
problems.solution: A difference of two squares always factors as (first root $+$ second root)(first root $-$ second root). Since $x^2-9=x^2-3^2$, the factors are $(x+3)$ and $(x-3)$. It is not $(x-3)^2$, because that would expand to $x^2-6x+9$.

problems.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $\dfrac{x^5\cdot x^3}{x^2}$ for $x\neq 0$?
problems.solution: Multiplying powers of the same base \emph{adds} exponents and dividing \emph{subtracts} them. Here $5+3=8$ and then $8-2=6$. Multiplying the exponents instead of adding them is what produces the larger choices.

problems.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $\dfrac{12x^5}{3x^2}$ for $x\neq 0$?
problems.solution: Divide the numerical coefficients and subtract the exponents separately: $12\div 3=4$ and $x^{5-2}=x^3$. The coefficients are divided, never subtracted, and the exponents are subtracted, never divided.

problems.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $6x^2+9x$?
problems.solution: Factoring out the greatest common factor is division: the GCF of $6x^2$ and $9x$ is $3x$, and dividing each term by $3x$ leaves $2x$ and $3$. Checking by redistributing is the fastest way to reject the other choices.
steps: The GCF of $6$ and $9$ is $3$; both terms contain $x$, so the GCF is $3x$.

problems.stem: Which of the following is equivalent to $x^2+7x+12$?
problems.solution: For a monic trinomial you need two numbers whose product is the constant term and whose sum is the middle coefficient. Here $3\cdot 4=12$ and $3+4=7$. The pair $(2,6)$ multiplies to $12$ but sums to $8$, which is why that choice fails.
steps: Look for two numbers with product $12$ and sum $7$.

problems.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $(2x-5)^2$?
problems.solution: Squaring a binomial is not squaring each term: $(a-b)^2=a^2-2ab+b^2$ carries a middle term. With $a=2x$ and $b=5$ the middle term is $-2(2x)(5)=-20x$; halving it to $-10x$ is the other common slip.

problems.stem: For $x\neq 4$, the expression $\dfrac{x^2-16}{x-4}$ is equivalent to $x+c$, where $c$ is a constant. What is the value of $c$?
problems.solution: You may cancel only a common \emph{factor}, so the numerator must be factored first. Since $x^2-16=(x+4)(x-4)$, the factor $x-4$ cancels and $x+4$ remains, giving $c=4$.

problems.stem: For $x\neq -2$, which expression is equivalent to $\dfrac{x^2+5x+6}{x+2}$?
problems.solution: Factor before you cancel. The numerator is $(x+2)(x+3)$, so the whole factor $x+2$ divides out and $x+3$ remains. Cancelling the loose $x$ in $x+2$ against the $x^2$ is not allowed, because $x+2$ is a sum, not a product.

problems.stem: For $x\neq 0$, which expression is equivalent to $\left(3x^{-2}\right)^{-1}$?
problems.solution: An outer exponent hits every factor inside, including the coefficient: $3^{-1}=\frac13$ and $\left(x^{-2}\right)^{-1}=x^{2}$. Leaving the $3$ untouched, or leaving $x$ in the denominator, are the two mistakes the distractors record.

problems.stem: What is the value of $16^{3/4}$?
problems.solution: A fractional exponent is a root and a power: the denominator gives the root, the numerator gives the power. Taking the fourth root first keeps the numbers small: $\sqrt[4]{16}=2$, then $2^3=8$.

problems.stem: For $x>0$, which expression is equivalent to $\sqrt{72x^2}$?
problems.solution: Pull out the largest perfect-square factor. Here $72=36\cdot 2$ and $x^2$ is already a perfect square, so $\sqrt{72x^2}=6x\sqrt{2}$. The square root of $x^2$ is $x$, not $x^2$.
steps: What is left under the radical is $2$, so the value is $6x\sqrt{2}$.
problems.verify:
a = symbols('a', positive=True)
x = symbols('x')
result = sqrt(72*a**2).subs(a, x)

problems.stem: For $x\neq 0$, which expression is equivalent to $\dfrac{1}{x}+\dfrac{1}{2x}$?
problems.solution: Fractions are added over a common denominator, never by adding denominators. Rewriting $\frac1x$ as $\frac{2}{2x}$ makes the sum $\frac{2}{2x}+\frac{1}{2x}=\frac{3}{2x}$.

problems.stem: Which of the following is equivalent to $2x^2+7x+3$?
problems.solution: When the leading coefficient is not $1$, the middle term mixes the outer and inner products. For $(2x+1)(x+3)$ the outer and inner products are $6x$ and $x$, which total $7x$; for $(2x+3)(x+1)$ they total $5x$, so that pairing fails.
steps: The factors must have the form $(2x+m)(x+n)$ with $mn=3$.

problems.stem: For $x\neq 2$ and $x\neq -2$, which expression is equivalent to $\dfrac{x+2}{x^2-4}$?
problems.solution: Factor the denominator as $(x+2)(x-2)$; the common factor $x+2$ cancels and leaves $\frac{1}{x-2}$. Cancelling the $2$ in the numerator against the $4$ in the denominator is illegal --- both are inside sums, not factors.

problems.stem: For $x\neq 2$ and $x\neq -3$, the expression $\dfrac{x^2-9}{x^2+x-6}$ is equivalent to $\dfrac{x-3}{x-c}$, where $c$ is a constant. What is the value of $c$?
problems.solution: Factor top and bottom completely before cancelling: $\frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{(x+3)(x-2)}$. Only the shared factor $x+3$ disappears, leaving $\frac{x-3}{x-2}$, so $c=2$.

problems.stem: For $x\neq 1$ and $x\neq -1$, which expression is equivalent to $\dfrac{1}{x-1}-\dfrac{1}{x+1}$?
problems.solution: The common denominator is $(x-1)(x+1)=x^2-1$. The numerators become $(x+1)-(x-1)=2$, and the minus sign must be distributed across both terms of the second numerator. Subtracting the numerators as $1-1=0$ ignores the rewriting step entirely.

problems.stem: For $x>0$, which expression is equivalent to $\left(8x^6\right)^{2/3}$?
problems.solution: The outside exponent applies to the coefficient and to the variable power: $8^{2/3}=\left(\sqrt[3]{8}\right)^2=4$ and $x^{6\cdot 2/3}=x^4$. Multiplying $8$ by $\frac23$, or adding the exponents instead of multiplying them, gives the wrong choices.
problems.verify:
a = symbols('a', positive=True)
x = symbols('x')
result = simplify((8*a**6)**Rational(2, 3)).subs(a, x)

problems.stem: The equation $(3x+a)(2x+b)=6x^2+19x+15$ is true for all $x$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers. What is the value of $a+b$?
problems.solution: Matching coefficients gives two conditions at once: $ab=15$ for the constant term and $2a+3b=19$ for the $x$ term. Only $a=5$, $b=3$ satisfies both, so a factor pair that gives the right constant is not enough --- it must also give the right middle term.
steps: The positive integer pair $a=5$, $b=3$ works, so $a+b=8$.

problems.stem: For $x\neq -5$, which expression is equivalent to $\dfrac{2x^2+7x-15}{x+5}$?
problems.solution: Factor the numerator as $(x+5)(2x-3)$ --- the pair that produces the middle term $7x$ from $10x-3x$. Cancelling $x+5$ leaves $2x-3$. Choosing $2x+3$ means the signs of the constant were never checked against $-15$.

problems.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $(x-4)(x+4)$?
problems.solution: The outer and inner products are $4x$ and $-4x$, which cancel; that is exactly why a sum times a difference of the same two terms is a difference of squares.

problems.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $2x(3x-7)+5x$?
problems.solution: Distribute first, then combine like terms. After distributing you have $6x^2-14x+5x$, and $-14x+5x=-9x$. Only terms with the same power of $x$ may be combined, so $6x^2$ stays alone.

problems.stem: The expression $x^2+10x+25$ is equivalent to $(x+k)^2$, where $k$ is a positive constant. What is the value of $k$?
problems.solution: A perfect-square trinomial has a constant equal to the square of $k$ and a middle coefficient equal to $2k$. Both tests agree here: $5^2=25$ and $2(5)=10$, so $k=5$.

problems.stem: Which of the following is equivalent to $4x^2-25$?
problems.solution: Both terms are perfect squares: $4x^2=(2x)^2$ and $25=5^2$. A difference of squares factors as $(2x+5)(2x-5)$; the squared forms are wrong because they would create a middle term.

problems.stem: For $x\neq 0$ and $y\neq 0$, which expression is equivalent to $\dfrac{x^4y^3}{xy^5}$?
problems.solution: Handle each base separately: $x^{4-1}=x^3$ and $y^{3-5}=y^{-2}$, and a negative exponent means the factor belongs in the denominator. Adding the $y$ exponents instead of subtracting them gives $y^8$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
result = simplify(x**4*y**3/(x*y**5))

problems.stem: What is the value of $27^{2/3}$?
problems.solution: The denominator of the exponent is the root and the numerator is the power. Taking the cube root first keeps the arithmetic small: $\sqrt[3]{27}=3$, and $3^2=9$.

problems.stem: Which expression shows $3x^2-12$ factored completely?
problems.solution: Always take the greatest common factor out first, then look again: $3x^2-12=3(x^2-4)$, and $x^2-4$ is still a difference of squares. Stopping at $3(x^2-4)$ leaves the factoring unfinished.

problems.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $(x+3)\left(x^2-2x+4\right)$?
problems.solution: Every term of the trinomial must be multiplied by $x$ and by $3$, giving six products before like terms are collected: $-2x^2+3x^2=x^2$ and $4x-6x=-2x$. Multiplying only matching-degree terms is what produces the other answers.

problems.stem: The equation $(2x-3)(3x+k)=6x^2+x-15$ is true for all values of $x$, where $k$ is a constant. What is the value of $k$?
problems.solution: Because the equation holds for every $x$, matching coefficients is legal. The constant term gives $-3k=-15$, so $k=5$, and the middle term confirms it: $2k-9=1$.
problems.verify:
x, k = symbols('x k')
result = solve(expand((2*x-3)*(3*x+k)) - (6*x**2+x-15), k)[0]

problems.stem: For $x\neq -3$, which expression is equivalent to $\dfrac{3x^2-27}{x+3}$?
problems.solution: Take out the common factor $3$ first, then recognise the difference of squares: $3(x-3)(x+3)$. After cancelling $x+3$ the $3$ must stay attached to both terms, giving $3x-9$ rather than $3x-27$.

problems.stem: For $x\neq 0$ and $x\neq -1$, which expression is equivalent to $\dfrac{2}{x+1}+\dfrac{3}{x}$?
problems.solution: The common denominator is the product $x(x+1)=x^2+x$. Each numerator must be scaled by what its denominator was missing: $2x$ and $3(x+1)$, whose sum is $5x+3$. Adding numerators and denominators straight across is the classic error.

problems.stem: For $x>0$, the expression $x^{1/2}\cdot x^{3/2}$ is equivalent to $x^{k}$, where $k$ is a constant. What is the value of $k$?
problems.solution: Powers of the same base multiply by adding exponents, and fractional exponents are added like ordinary fractions: $\frac12+\frac32=\frac42=2$. Multiplying the exponents would give $\frac34$, which is not what the product rule says.

problems.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $\sqrt{48}-\sqrt{12}$?
problems.solution: Radicals combine only after they are simplified to the same radicand: $\sqrt{48}=4\sqrt3$ and $\sqrt{12}=2\sqrt3$, so the difference is $2\sqrt3$. Subtracting under one radical sign, $\sqrt{48-12}=6$, is not a legal move.

problems.stem: For $x\neq 0$ and $y\neq 0$, which expression is equivalent to $\left(2x^3y^{-2}\right)^3$?
problems.solution: A power of a product raises each factor: $2^3=8$, $\left(x^3\right)^3=x^9$, and $\left(y^{-2}\right)^3=y^{-6}$, which moves to the denominator. Multiplying the coefficient by the exponent instead of raising it gives $6$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
result = simplify((2*x**3*y**(-2))**3)

problems.stem: For $x\neq 3$, which expression is equivalent to $\dfrac{x^2-5x+6}{x-3}$?
problems.solution: The numerator factors as $(x-2)(x-3)$, since $(-2)(-3)=6$ and $-2-3=-5$. Cancelling $x-3$ leaves $x-2$; the leftover factor is the one you did \emph{not} cancel.

problems.stem: Which of the following is equivalent to $6x^2-x-15$?
problems.solution: Split the middle term using two numbers with product $6(-15)=-90$ and sum $-1$: those are $9$ and $-10$. Grouping then gives $(2x+3)(3x-5)$; swapping the signs produces $x$ instead of $-x$ in the middle.
steps: Look for two numbers with product $-90$ and sum $-1$: $9$ and $-10$.

problems.stem: For $x\neq 1$ and $x\neq -3$, which expression is equivalent to $\dfrac{x^2-1}{x+3}\cdot\dfrac{x^2+3x}{x-1}$?
problems.solution: Factor every piece before multiplying: $\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x+3}\cdot\frac{x(x+3)}{x-1}$. Both $x-1$ and $x+3$ cancel diagonally, leaving $x(x+1)=x^2+x$. Cancelling before factoring would strand the $x+3$ in the denominator.

problems.stem: For $x\neq \tfrac12$, the expression $\dfrac{2x^2+5x-3}{2x-1}$ is equivalent to $x+c$, where $c$ is a constant. What is the value of $c$?
problems.solution: The numerator factors as $(2x-1)(x+3)$: the constant $-3$ comes from $(-1)(3)$ and the middle term from $6x-x=5x$. Cancelling $2x-1$ leaves $x+3$, so $c=3$.

problems.stem: For nonzero values of $x$ and $y$, which expression is equivalent to $\dfrac{1}{x^{-1}+y^{-1}}$?
problems.solution: Rewrite the negative exponents as fractions first: $\frac1x+\frac1y=\frac{y+x}{xy}$. The whole expression is the reciprocal of that sum, which flips it to $\frac{xy}{x+y}$. Turning $\frac{1}{x^{-1}+y^{-1}}$ into $x+y$ treats a sum of reciprocals as the reciprocal of a sum.
steps: Dividing $1$ by that fraction flips it.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
result = simplify(1/(x**(-1) + y**(-1)))

problems.stem: The expression $(2x+3)^2-(2x-3)^2$ is equivalent to $kx$, where $k$ is a constant. What is the value of $k$?
problems.solution: Expanding both squares gives $\left(4x^2+12x+9\right)-\left(4x^2-12x+9\right)$; the $4x^2$ and $9$ cancel and the two middle terms add, leaving $24x$. Forgetting to distribute the minus sign over all three terms of the second square is what loses half of that.

problems.stem: For $x\neq 2$ and $x\neq -2$, which expression is equivalent to $\dfrac{x^2-x-6}{x^2-4}$?
problems.solution: Factor both parts: $\frac{(x-3)(x+2)}{(x+2)(x-2)}$. Only $x+2$ is common, so it alone cancels and $\frac{x-3}{x-2}$ remains. Cancelling the $x^2$ terms first is the trap, because they are terms of a sum, not factors.

problems.stem: For $x\neq 1$ and $x\neq -1$, which expression is equivalent to $\dfrac{x}{x-1}-\dfrac{1}{x+1}$?
problems.solution: Over the common denominator $x^2-1$ the numerator is $x(x+1)-(x-1)=x^2+x-x+1=x^2+1$. The subtraction sign must reach both terms of $x-1$; dropping it on the $-1$ leaves $x^2+x-1$ instead.
steps: That simplifies to $x^2+1$, so the difference is $\dfrac{x^2+1}{x^2-1}$.
